edges.effect_quant: Cochrane reviews of ovulation induction in PCOS support a modest reproductive benefit from metformin, particularly in selected subfertility settings and in combination approaches, rather than a universal dramatic effect. The signal is real but context-dependent: metformin is not the strongest ovulation agent in every comparison, yet it often improves ovulation-related outcomes relative to doing less metabolically targeted treatment.
edges.population: women with polycystic ovary syndrome and oligo-ovulation or anovulation undergoing ovulation-induction treatment
edges.mechanism: Metformin may improve ovulation in PCOS by reducing insulin resistance and lowering the hyperinsulinemic drive that amplifies ovarian androgen production and disrupts follicular maturation. The result is usually a partial restoration of ovulatory function rather than a guaranteed standalone fertility solution.
edges.summary: Metformin can improve ovulation rate in women with PCOS, but the benefit is modest and depends on the treatment setting. The best synthesis supports a real ovulation signal, especially in subfertility and combination-treatment pathways, while also showing that metformin is not automatically superior to every dedicated ovulation-induction strategy.
edges.caveats: This edge should not be oversold as a one-size-fits-all fertility fix: comparative effectiveness shifts depending on whether metformin is used alone, with clomiphene, or with gonadotropins. Its value is often greatest when metabolic dysfunction is part of the reproductive problem rather than when rapid ovulation induction alone is the goal.
